results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Bringer of the Last Gift, Superior Spider-Man and Town Greeter.
results.text:
The deck is submitted as a brew: a Golgari (black-green) mill-and-ramp shell from the Golgari Roots list with a blue splash for Superior Spider-Man. I considered three directions. A Dimir build would have dropped Town Greeter and the mill plan. A Simic build can't cast Bringer, which needs BB. I chose Golgari because Town Greeter, Llanowar Elves, Molt Tender and Overlord fill graveyards with creatures and ramp toward the 8-drop.

The plan is to fill the graveyard early with Town Greeter and Overlord, which also returns Bringer to hand. Then hard-cast Bringer on about turn 7 to wipe both boards and return every creature from both graveyards, and copy the best one with Spider-Man. Removal (Feed the Swarm, Assassin's Trophy, Bitter Triumph, Murder) covers the early game against Izzet and Vivi.

Honest caveat: the tool estimates the full win line is drawn by turn 7 in only about 3.8% of games, so this is a grindy, speculative deck and not a proven list. Two cards I kept despite low recent play, Feed the Swarm and Assassin's Trophy, are justified in the card notes; I swapped out Quag Feast for Murder. The 15-card sideboard leans on hard removal and Massacre Wurm against the aggro decks.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Mightform Harmonizer, Spell Snare and Full Bore.
results.text:
I built a green-red landfall deck, with a light blue splash for Spell Snare. It was the only direction where Mightform Harmonizer and Full Bore both work. A Simic build would have dropped Full Bore, and an Izzet build would have dropped Harmonizer, since its GG cost doesn't fit.

The plan is to play Bristly Bill and Mossborn Hydra early so their landfall counters grow the Hydra. Harmonizer then doubles its power on a land drop, and Full Bore adds +3/+2 for the attack. Abrade, Obliterating Bolt and Lightning Strike handle the opposing creatures. Spell Snare is the weakest card in the deck and is in only for the requested card.

The landfall shell and its fetch lands came from the Landfall list, and the removal suite follows the most-played Abrade and Obliterating Bolt in the field. No published list runs all three requested cards together, so this is a brew. On the play, Harmonizer and Full Bore each show up by turn 5 about 57% of the time, and all three together only about 9%. The deck runs 18 lands plus 4 Llanowar Elves, which is more than the checker's generic count for a low curve, because landfall needs land drops.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Airbender Ascension, Bramble Familiar and Appa, Steadfast Guardian.
results.text:
I built a G/W brew (`brew`, donor shell: Selesnya Offense) that ramps into Appa and uses Airbender Ascension to keep removing blockers. Odds are modest: Appa is in hand or castable by turn 4 about 31% of the time on the play, and the full line is drawn by turn 5 in only about 2% of games.

I considered three directions:
- **G/W ramp with Appa and Ascension (chosen):** Bramble Familiar and Llanowar Elves make Appa and Elspeth castable on time, and Selesnya Offense's creatures and Innkeeper's Talent fill the curve.
- **W/U airbend flicker:** Aang, Swift Savior, Aang the Last Airbender and Airbending Lesson build around blinking, but the deck would have less ramp and need a blue base.
- **Blue-splash Rogue-style Aang deck:** this is what the Rogue lists actually run; I passed on it because the splash makes Appa and Elspeth less reliable.

I chose G/W because the green ramp is the most reliable way to reach Appa on curve. The plan is to land Airbender Ascension early to exile their best creature, then flash in Appa to exile Ascension and recast it for {2}. Each recast makes an Ally token and re-triggers Ascension's airbend, and Elspeth on turn 5 doubles the tokens for the win.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Abandon Attachments, Firebending Lesson and Combustion Technique.
results.text:
I built a mono-red Lesson deck with the Izzet/Boros burn-and-threat core. The plan is to curve out with cheap attackers and burn, then use Firebending Lesson and Abandon Attachments to fill the graveyard so Combustion Technique can exile a blocker or a larger threat. Nova Hellkite and Tersa Lightshatter close the game.

I weighed three directions:
- **Mono-red Lessons with the Izzet burn core (chosen):** Mono-Red is the only Standard shell running all three cards, though it appears in just 2 lists. Its mana is clean and its Lesson package works, and the burn core is the most-played part of the field.
- **Izzet Lessons:** Blue Lessons like Accumulate Wisdom and Boomerang Basics would thin the deck less than red Lessons and would make the mana worse.
- **Boros Lessons:** The white Lessons (Airbender's Reversal, Airbending Lesson, Enter the Avatar State, Yip Yip!) have no results in the last 90 days, so this direction was too thin.

Two changes from the tools shaped the final list. Screaming Nemesis is banned in Standard, so the Izzet and Boros lists in the meta data are not usable as-is. Bonehoard Dracosaur was flagged as unplayed in recent Standard lists, so I replaced it with Stadium Headliner and Witchstalker Frenzy. The deck runs 17 lands, which is below the checker's 22-land recommendation for this format. I kept it low because the curve is so cheap (average mana value about 1.8), and Soulstone Sanctuary and the kicker costs give it mana sinks.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Ashling, Rekindled, Sunderflock and Bounce Off.
results.text:
I built a blue-red Elemental deck that uses Sunderflock as a one-sided reset. Every creature in it is an Elemental, so Sunderflock bounces only the opponent's non-Elementals. Ashling ramps into 5-6 drops, and Sunderflock costs about three mana once an MV-6 Elemental like Ice Flan is on the battlefield.

I considered three directions. The Rogue lists that run Sunderflock and Ashling are green-blue creature decks, where Sunderflock would bounce their own creatures. The Simic Ouroboroid package, which runs Bounce Off, is a non-Elemental board that Sunderflock also punishes. The blue-red Elemental build was the strongest because the whole creature suite is Elementals. The deck is a brew, not a proven list.

The line is Ashling on turn 2, Wistfulness on turn 4 (paid with Ashling's mana), Ice Flan on turn 5, then Sunderflock on turn 6 for about three mana, then attack. That line is fragile: the simulator put the chance of drawing every card in it by turn 6 at 3.2%. The deck runs 17 lands and the checker still flags it as light, but the two Stratosoarer landcyclers and two Ice Flan islandcyclers help cover that.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Resonating Lute, Inevitable Defeat and Jeskai Revelation.

results.prompt: Brew me a Standard deck built around Greedy Freebooter, The Sackville-Bagginses and Umbral Collar Zealot.
results.text:
I'll start by checking the three named cards and how they're played.

The three cards are a sacrifice package: Freebooter and Sackville-Bagginses both want creatures or artifacts to die or be sacrificed, and Zealot is a sacrifice outlet. No published list plays them together. I'll look at the field and search for sacrifice enablers.

Sacrifice synergy is real in Standard, and the field has black support for it. I'll pull the black sacrifice and death-trigger cards that fit alongside the three named cards.

Here are three directions I can build from the pool and the field:

1. **Black sacrifice aristocrats**: mostly black, with Liliana, Sephiroth, Vengeful Bloodwitch, and Corrupted Conviction as payoffs and fodder.
2. **Dimir sacrifice**: borrow Dimir Midrange's blue-black mana and its interaction (Bitter Triumph, Requiting Hex, Tishana's Tidebinder) around the same sacrifice engine.
3. **Mardu-style recursion**: borrow Mardu Discard's Bloodghast and Iron-Shield Elf package for repeatable sacrifice fodder.

Before picking, I'll confirm the legality and text of the key cards in each direction.

I'm going mono-black. The strongest black removal in the field (Bitter Triumph and Requiting Hex, both on the Dimir and Mardu lists) is already black, so the Dimir blue splash isn't needed. Bloodghast gives recurring sacrifice fodder from the Mardu package. Next I'll check the deck's mana and odds.

The main deck checks clean: 60 cards, 23 lands, 25 black sources, and the odds of a black source by turn 3 are 99%. I'll check the sideboard against the field, which is full of small creatures (Prowess, Landfall, Selesnya, Elementals) and grindy control (Excruciator, 4C, Lifegain).

The sideboard came in at 10 cards, so I'll fill it to 15 with the sacrifice-synergy creatures I've already seen, after confirming their legality.

All 15 sideboard slots check out, so the deck is ready to submit.

I built a mono-black sacrifice deck around the three cards and submitted it. No published list plays these together, so this is untested.

**Directions I considered:**
1. **Mono-black sacrifice (chosen):** Freebooter, Sackville-Bagginses and Zealot are all black, and Bitter Triumph and Requiting Hex are both black, so the deck gets its best removal without a second colour.
2. **Dimir sacrifice:** Borrowing Dimir Midrange's blue-black mana and interaction works, but the blue cards add nothing the sacrifice plan needs.
3. **Mardu recursion:** Bloodghast gives repeatable fodder, but it needs red and white. I took Bloodghast alone and kept the deck mono-black.

**The plan:** Turn 1 Freebooter, turn 3 Sackville sacrificing Freebooter for a card and a Treasure, then Zealot as a free sacrifice outlet. Every death (Bloodghast, Treasures, zombies) drains the opponent through Vengeful Bloodwitch and draws cards through Liliana, with Vein Ripper as the finisher. Bitter Triumph, Requiting Hex and Hunt the Mark handle their early threats.

**Mana and odds:** 23 lands (22 Swamp and Midgar, City of Mako), giving a black source by turn 3 with 99% odds. The deck is consistent, but the full turn-6 line (every named card drawn) has only about 0.6% odds. Treat it as a deck to test and tune, not a proven list.

**Field context:** Prowess and Landfall are the two largest strategies (17% and 15%), and both are built around small creatures, so the sideboard leans on Massacre Girl, Massacre Wurm and Blasphemous Edict.

The plan is to play cheap prowess threats, clear blockers with Combustion Technique and Reckless Rage, filter with Abandon Attachments, and finish with Screaming Nemesis or burn to the face. The line I submitted wins on turn 5 at the earliest, and the deck is not built for fast kills.

The main risk is that Igneous Inspiration and Combustion Technique are narrow, with 0 real lists for the former, so the deck runs them at 3 and 2 copies rather than 4. 2. **Amulet Titan (G/R)** with Fight Rigging bolted on. This is proven, but Trudge and Symbiosis fit poorly and Amulet's land plan doesn't use Fight Rigging.
3. **G/U Neoform** with Eldritch Evolution and counters. Blue adds mana strain, and the deck needs no interaction to make Fight Rigging's free spell work.

I'll build direction 1. Next I'll confirm the rest of the cards I plan to use.

Every card I plan to use is legal and tool-confirmed. Next I'll run a first check on the 60-card build.

The checker counts 18 lands (17 Forest plus 2 Symbiosis MDFCs) against a recommended 20.8. Its Amulet comparison is off, since Amulet runs about 31 lands with Urza's Saga. I'll move one more land in and cut Sakura-Tribe Elder, then recheck.

The check is clean: no errors and no warnings. Next I'll size the opening-turn line, which needs Fight Rigging, Trudge and a mana source.

Before I submit, I'll confirm the sideboard cards the Modern field calls for: artifact removal against Affinity, Tron and Belcher, cheap instant removal, and protection.

The Modern-legal sideboard cards are confirmed. Here's the submission: a mono-green Fight Rigging ramp brew with 15 sideboard cards against the field's artifact decks, Dismember and Veil of Summer.

I built a mono-green brew around Fight Rigging. Slumbering Trudge is the enabler: cast with X=3 it is an untapped 6/6, and one Fight Rigging counter makes it 7 power, which unlocks the hideaway card for free. Turntimber Symbiosis is a late-game creature finder and doubles as a land, and the deck is backed by mana elves, Badgermole Cub, Green Sun's Zenith, Primeval Titan and Ghalta.

I chose this over an Amulet Titan (G/R) build and a G/U Neoform build. Amulet Titan's land plan doesn't use Fight Rigging, and blue adds mana strain without helping the free-spell engine. results.prompt: Brew me a Legacy deck built around Apex Devastator, Call Forth the Tempest and Creative Technique.
results.text:

The cheat shell won because Show and Tell, Sneak Attack and Omniscience put fatties and Omniscience into play without paying mana costs, and Creative Technique can cast Apex Devastator and Call Forth the Tempest for free. That also means the deck needs no green mana. Sneak and Show went 5-0 at Legacy League 2025-09-09.

**The plan:** Dig with Brainstorm, Ponder and Stock Up for Show and Tell plus a fatty, usually Emrakul. Show and Tell puts Emrakul into play for 2U, and annihilator 6 with 15 flying damage closes the game. Creative Technique and Omniscience are backup routes that free-cast Apex Devastator or Call Forth the Tempest.

**Honest odds:** Show and Tell and Emrakul together by turn 4 on the play are about 21% with no card draw counted. The full win line is drawn by turn 4 in about 9% of games.

- Apex Devastator and Call Forth run only 2 copies each because they cost 8 to 10 mana.
- The 15-card sideboard is aimed at the field: Pyroblast and Force of Negation against blue tempo, Grafdigger's Cage against reanimation, and Fury and Brotherhood's End for the creature decks.

The Legacy list is an artifact-combo shell, and the Vintage field is dominated by Force of Will, Mental Misstep and Psychic Frog decks. Before choosing a direction, I'll check the engine and the Vintage-legal pieces I might use.

The engine and key Vintage pieces are confirmed as legal. Next I'll check the supporting cards I'm considering so every card fact comes from the tools.

The first check flagged only the land count, and it counts cheap spells as ramp. My deck has about 22 mana sources in total, so I'll shift the two rocks for lands and check again.

The warning is still there. I'll check how many lands the proven Vintage lists in this same field run before deciding whether to add more.

Proven Vintage lists run about 14–15 lands, but they cast expensive spells that my combo never needs. My cost curve is almost all 0–2 mana, the loop itself costs no mana, and I have about 11 free or near-free accelerants, so I'll keep 11 lands and say so. Next I'll check sideboard candidates against the field's main threats.

Sideboard candidates are settled. Mindbreak Trap, Abrade, Tormod's Crypt and Pyroblast-style blue hate all hit cards this field plays heavily. I'll run the full 60 plus 15 through the checker.

The checker passes with one warning, which I've justified above. Submitting the deck now.

The checker flagged Ichor Wellspring as a rarely played card. It has a specific job here, so I'll keep it and explain why.

Submitted as a brew: a blue-red Vintage deck built around the Welder–Cam–Extruder loop. Goblin Engineer tutors Sewer-veillance Cam into the graveyard. Then Goblin Welder sacrifices Legion Extruder to return Cam, and Cam's enter and leave triggers untap Welder. Welder then sacrifices Cam to return Extruder, which deals 2 damage each cycle. The loop costs no mana, so it is lethal from 20 life in ten cycles. Force of Will, Force of Negation and Mental Misstep protect the setup.

I chose this over two other directions. One was the red Legacy Sewer list, which I borrowed the engine from but dropped for its 21 lands and weaker fillers. The other was a blue Tinker-style artifact shell with no loop. The Vintage-power loop with a counter suite was the strongest use of the three cards.

The checker flagged 11 lands against a recommended ~20. I kept 11 because the list is almost all 0–2 mana, the loop itself costs nothing, and the field's proven lists run 14–15 lands only because they cast expensive spells. I kept Ichor Wellspring on purpose: Welder or Engineer can return it repeatedly for cards, which is a backup if the loop is stopped.

Living Death itself is a one-of tech in those lists, so this build commits to it harder than any real list does.

**The plan:** Living Death is symmetric, so this deck wants creatures in its own graveyard and a board that is worse than the opponent's. Survival of the Fittest and Animate Dead put big creatures in the yard, and Living Death returns them with their enter-the-battlefield triggers (Nekrataal, Phyrexian Delver, Gravedigger, Bone Shredder, Wall of Blossoms, Deranged Hermit). Duress and Cabal Therapy strip the opponent's answers, and Terror, Snuff Out and Nekrataal handle creatures until the reset. Chainer, Dementia Master gives a late-game reanimation engine. The deck runs 22 lands (9 Swamp, 9 Forest, 4 Llanowar Wastes) plus 4 Birds of Paradise.

**Honest caveat:** Living Death is a five-mana sorcery that only pays off when the board and graveyards line up. Draw odds show about 46% to have at least one copy by turn 5 on the play, and the winning line needs Survival of the Fittest and a creature in the yard. The 15-card sideboard covers the field's most-played decks.
